details: Three categories of Chernobyl first responders: (1) Plant operators on shift (Alexander Akimov shift; ~20 personnel in control room vicinity); (2) Chernobyl NPP fire brigade (Lieutenant Pravik team; ~30 firefighters); (3) Pripyat city fire brigade (Major Telyatnikov; additional ~100 firefighters); total initially responding: ~130-150 persons; firefighters reached site within 6-7 minutes of 01:23 alarm; worked on burning roofs (Turbine Hall and Unit 3 roof) without respirators
medical_significance: Firefighters working on contaminated graphite debris without any respiratory protection; received external whole-body doses from graphite fragments; beta burns to all exposed skin from surface contamination; some picked up graphite fragments by hand (later reports); dose rates on roof surface >100 Gy/hr; exposure time 45-90 minutes on roof → individual doses 2-16 Gy for those on roof
source: ars_cases_REAL.csv; Gale 1988 Nature; Guskova 2001 J Radiol Prot; Mettler 1992; Mould 2000

details: Acute Radiation Syndrome: 134 confirmed cases (UNSCEAR criteria: dose >1 Gy with clinical ARS signs); 28 deaths within first 3 months (all from ARS or ARS complications); degree I (1-2 Gy): 41 cases; degree II (2-4 Gy): 50 cases; degree III (4-6 Gy): 22 cases; degree IV (>6 Gy): 21 cases; degrees III-IV = highest mortality; see ars_cases_REAL.csv for complete data
medical_significance: 134 ARS cases from a single accident = unprecedented in peacetime nuclear history; all ARS cases were from first responders and plant workers in first hours; NO ARS cases among general public (too distant/low dose); ARS degree IV (>6 Gy): survival required bone marrow transplant or spontaneous marrow recovery; 2 accidental fatal criticalities had ARS in individuals (SL-1 1961; Tokaimura 1999)
source: ars_cases_REAL.csv; Guskova Baranov 1988 J Radiol Prot; UNSCEAR 2008; Mettler 1992 Radiology

details: Hospital No. 6 (Moscow Clinical Hospital No. 6): Soviet/Russian specialized facility for radiation injuries; associated with Biophysics Institute; chief specialist: Dr. Angelina Guskova (world's leading expert on ARS); deputy: Dr. Alexander Baranov; 134 confirmed ARS patients evacuated by specially chartered flights from Kyiv to Moscow; first arrivals April 27 (within 24 hours of accident); 237 patients initially hospitalized (134 confirmed ARS; remainder initial suspicion)
medical_significance: 237 initially hospitalized; 103 later discharged without ARS diagnosis; 134 confirmed; demonstrates: diagnosis of ARS is clinical (requires time for lymphocyte kinetics + symptom development); cannot be determined from single radiation measurement; Dr. Guskova's team performed all dose reconstructions from: lymphocyte counts; skin burn patterns; beta burn distribution; clinical symptoms
source: Guskova Baranov 1988; Baranov 1989 BMT; Mould 2000; ars_cases_REAL.csv

details: Dr. Angelina Guskova (1924-2015): head of radiation medicine clinic at Hospital No. 6; treated all 134 ARS patients 1986; previously treated Kyshtym and other Soviet radiation accidents; developed Soviet ARS grading system; assessed cases by: lymphocyte nadir at 7-9 days; onset of nausea/vomiting (within 4 hours → high dose); skin erythema; hair loss onset; worked 20-hour days April-June 1986; published seminal 1988 paper in J Radiol Prot
medical_significance: Guskova's clinical skill critical: had to distinguish true ARS from anxiety/emotional response in hundreds of people claiming exposure; no real-time dosimetry for most patients; lymphocyte count at 24-48 hours was most reliable early biological dose indicator; CD4/CD8 ratio changes helped characterize immune suppression; lymphocyte nadir timing predicted marrow recovery window
source: Guskova Baranov 1988 J Radiol Prot PMID:3184487; Mettler 1992; UNSCEAR 2008

details: Biological dosimetry using lymphocyte count: normal count 1500-4000/µL; after whole-body irradiation: lymphocytes die within hours-days (mitotic death); nadir at day 7-9 post-exposure; nadir count correlates with dose: >1000/µL (not significant); 500-1000/µL (~1-2 Gy); 100-500/µL (~2-4 Gy); <100/µL (>4-6 Gy); <50/µL (>6 Gy; potentially lethal without BMT); serial counts also show recovery kinetics
medical_significance: Lymphocyte kinetics were PRIMARY biological dosimetry tool for Chernobyl ARS cases; physical dosimetry (pocket dosimeters) mostly unavailable/falsified; EPR tooth enamel retrospective but not available in 1986; FISH cytogenetics not routine in 1986; lymphocyte count + skin burn distribution + symptom onset time = clinical dose reconstruction method
source: Guskova 1988; Bond 1965 Radiation Injury in Man; Goans 1997 Health Phys; retrospective_dosimetry_methods_REAL.csv

details: BMT (Bone Marrow Transplant) at Hospital No. 6: 13 BMT performed; donor: Robert Gale (UCLA) with Soviet team; Dr. Gale flew to Moscow April 28 with cyclosporine A (not available in USSR); 13 allogeneic BMT; results: only 2 successful engraftments; 11 failed (graft rejection); of 2 engrafted: both eventually died from complications; none of the 13 BMT patients survived long-term; those who survived ARS did so via spontaneous marrow recovery
medical_significance: BMT failure rate: 11/13 graft rejection; retrospective analysis showed BMT was wrong treatment for most Chernobyl ARS cases; reason: dose reconstruction showed most patients had mixed exposure (whole body AND localized skin/soft tissue); also: Chernobyl patients had combined radiation+thermal burns (burns suppress immune engraftment); BMT appropriate for pure whole-body irradiation above ~5-6 Gy with NO bone marrow recovery; Chernobyl patients had heterogeneous dose distribution
source: Baranov 1989 Bone Marrow Transplantation 4:69-76; Gale Butturini 1992; Champlin 1988 BMT; ars_cases_REAL.csv

details: Beta radiation burns (cutaneous radiation injury): beta particles from graphite/fuel dust on skin; depth of beta penetration < 2mm for lower-energy beta (Sr-90); up to 11mm for Y-90 (2.28 MeV); skin layers: epidermis ~0.1mm; dermis 1-2mm; subcutaneous fat 10-20mm; beta from fuel particles causes: early erythema (hours); dry desquamation (weeks); moist desquamation (skin breakdown); with high dose: deep tissue necrosis; some patients had >100% of BSA (body surface area) with some degree of beta burn
medical_significance: Combined radiation injury = whole-body gamma/neutron dose + localized beta burns; beta burns initially mimic thermal burns but: no immediate pain; onset at 1-2 hours (early erythema); much deeper and harder to treat; surgical excision of necrotic tissue required in severe cases; some patients required skin grafting; 20 of 28 ARS deaths had severe beta burn component contributing to death
source: Hopewell 1990 PMID:2239088; Mettler 1992; Peter 1994; ars_cases_REAL.csv; beta_alpha_radiation_physics_REAL.csv

details: ARS clinical timeline: Prodromal phase (0-2 days): nausea, vomiting, erythema; if vomiting within 1 hour → dose likely >4 Gy; if 1-4 hours → 2-4 Gy; if >6 hours → <2 Gy; Latent phase (1-3 weeks): apparent recovery; Manifest illness phase (2-4 weeks): fever, infection, hemorrhage, hair loss; Recovery/death (4-8 weeks); ARS stages reflect: lymphoid tissue depletion; bone marrow failure; gut epithelium damage (>6 Gy); neurovascular syndrome (>20 Gy)
medical_significance: Time to vomiting = simple clinical triage tool for mass casualty nuclear events; most reliable indicator when no dosimetry available; Chernobyl firefighters arriving at Hospital No. 6: triage based on: time to first vomiting; skin erythema pattern; lymphocyte count 24hr; combination → clinical dose estimate within factor of 2; time-to-vomiting used in REAC/TS (Oak Ridge) nuclear accident response protocols to this day
source: REAC/TS protocol; Goans 1997 Health Phys; Dainiak 2012 Blood; Guskova 1988

details: 28 deaths from ARS within first 3 months: first death: Vladimir Shashenok (shift adjuster; killed by explosion/crushing injuries April 26); second death: Valery Khodemchuk (pump operator; body never recovered; entombed in reactor); subsequent ARS deaths April through August 1986; final ARS-attributed deaths by approximately September-October 1986; total confirmed ARS deaths by end 1986: 28; 2 additional deaths from explosion/physical trauma
medical_significance: Plant director Bryukhanov's dosimetry report to Moscow stated maximum dose 3.6 R/hr (=3.6 mSv/hr) — instruments topped out at 3.6 R = scale maximum; actual dose rates were 100-1000x higher (>1 Gy/hr on roof); deliberate underreporting or instrument saturation? Both; explains why initial Soviet response was inadequate — authorities believed their own false instruments
source: UNSCEAR 2008; ars_cases_REAL.csv; Mould 2000 Chernobyl Record; Plokhy 2018 Chernobyl

details: I-131 thyroid doses in ARS patients: NOT systematically measured in acute phase; patients were high-dose whole-body (ARS) — thyroid dose was additional but overshadowed by bone marrow/skin failure; retrospective reconstruction of I-131 thyroid doses in ARS patients impossible due to: rapid decay (t1/2=8.02d); no in vivo thyroid counting in first days; thyroid doses in ARS patients likely high (same CEZ contamination) but thyroid cancer risk irrelevant given severe ARS injuries
medical_significance: Contrast: systematic thyroid dose measurement performed for evacuees and general population (but poorly, as documented in retrospective_dosimetry_methods_REAL.csv); for ARS patients thyroid dose was secondary medical concern; however long-term thyroid cancer monitoring of ARS survivors conducted by UNSCEAR follow-up; 5 ARS survivors developed thyroid cancer (background rate not excluded)

details: Medpunkt (medical point) at Pripyat and Chernobyl NPP Medical Unit (Medchast No. 126): received first cases immediately; Medchast No. 126 chief: Dr. Leonid Hamyanyuk; received ~100 patients first hours; initial diagnosis for many: 'vegetovascular dystonia' (stress disorder) — misdiagnosis of radiation sickness as psychological; 100+ patients transferred overnight to Hospital No. 6 Moscow; Pripyat hospital overwhelmed by 0400
medical_significance: Medchast No. 126 not equipped for radiation triage; no geiger counters on medical staff; staff themselves contaminated by patients (secondary contamination); first diagnostic error: attributing vomiting to stress/alcohol; this delayed appropriate isolation/decontamination; patients' contaminated clothing left in hospital basement (massive localized contamination source for years)
source: Mould 2000; Read 1993 Ablaze; Plokhy 2018; IAEA 2006 Chernobyl Legacy

details: Potassium iodide (KI) tablets: stable iodine blocks thyroid uptake of I-131 (>90% reduction if taken before exposure); ZNPP medical unit had KI stockpile; NOT distributed to Pripyat residents; not distributed to firefighters; Polish government distributed 18 million KI doses April 28-29; Soviet KI distribution: some workers at NPP received KI; general Pripyat population (49,360) received NO KI in first 36 hours; children who received milk in first hours received highest thyroid doses
medical_significance: KI non-distribution = major preventable health failure; UNSCEAR estimates thyroid doses 30-60% lower if KI distributed at evacuation (April 27) rather than not at all; combination of KI + early evacuation + milk ban = could have prevented majority of thyroid cancers in children; Polish example proves rapid distribution possible; Soviet failure was administrative/secrecy not logistical

details: Lieutenant Viktor Pravik (Chernobyl NPP fire brigade; 23 years old): arrived on roof within 6 minutes; died May 11 1986 from ARS degree IV (dose ~16 Gy estimated); Lieutenant Leonid Telyatnikov (Pripyat city fire brigade): arrived with second team; received dose ~4-6 Gy; survived ARS (rare degree III/IV survivor); hair loss; multiple hospitalizations; died 2004 from lung cancer (possibly radiation-related); Pravik's team was the first group to arrive on the burning roof
medical_significance: Pravik and team were on highly contaminated Unit 3 roof (containing fragments of fuel assemblies blown from Unit 4); actual dose rates on roof measured retrospectively 100-500 Gy/hr in hottest spots; workers stayed 45-90 minutes; received cumulative doses 2-16 Gy depending on exact location; complete human exposure record impossible to reconstruct
source: Mould 2000; Read 1993; UNSCEAR 2008; ars_cases_REAL.csv; Plokhy 2018 Chernobyl

details: Alexander Akimov (senior reactor control engineer; shift leader): followed orders to press AZ-5; then manually opened feedwater valves believing reactor core had not been damaged; worked in highly contaminated locations for hours believing reactor intact; dose estimated 9-12 Gy; died May 11 1986 ARS degree IV; Leonid Toptunov (reactor control operator; 26 years old): pressed AZ-5 button at 01:23:40 when ordered by Dyatlov; dose estimated 12-16 Gy; died May 14 1986
medical_significance: Akimov/Toptunov continued trying to provide cooling water for hours post-accident not knowing reactor was destroyed; both had been following procedures (within the flawed test); moral complexity: pressed SCRAM button (AZ-5) when ordered AND the AZ-5 caused the excursion due to graphite tip; worked to death trying to save reactor they didn't know was already destroyed; both posthumously recognized as victims not perpetrators
source: Read 1993 Ablaze; Plokhy 2018; Mould 2000; INSAG-7; chernobyl_accident_chronology_REAL.csv

details: Long-term outcomes of 134 ARS survivors: degree I (n=41): all survived; degree II (n=50): all survived; degree III (n=22): 1 died (acute); degree IV (n=21): 17 died acutely; 4 survived; long-term: survivors monitored continuously; increased leukemia risk (ERR/Gy=1.26); cataract risk; CVD risk; no statistically confirmed excess solid tumors at these doses (too few persons; too short follow-up); some survivors with severe beta burns have chronic skin problems
medical_significance: 134 ARS cases → 106 long-term survivors; largest single cohort of high-dose radiation accident survivors in history; critical contribution to radiation medicine: showed that even 4-6 Gy exposure can be survived with intensive supportive care (transfusions, antibiotics, G-CSF growth factors); modern protocols developed from Chernobyl experience used in subsequent accidents (Goiania 1987, Tokaimura 1999)
source: Guskova 2001 J Radiol Prot; UNSCEAR 2008; liquidator_health_outcomes_REAL.csv; ars_cases_REAL.csv
